articles.title: The last days of Joe Louis, and the terrible cost of greatness: Louis vs. Rocky Marciano, 75 years later
articles.summary: In a segregated America, Joe Louis became something extraordinary: a Black heavyweight champion celebrated as a national hero, who gave his country everythin...
articles.body:
When it was over, America's hero lay more out of the ring than in it. Body sprawled on the apron. One foot hooked over the bottom rope. His head hanging over the edge as sportswriters at ringside reached up to keep him from falling to the floor. His bald spot was on prominent display, as if the world needed another reminder that the ravages of time had brought him here as much as that final right hand that put him all the way out.

But that's not completely true. The fact is Joe Louis probably never would been in that ring at all if he weren't so deeply in debt to the United States government. His service during World War II, once lauded as so vital to America's war effort, wasn't enough to keep the Internal Revenue Service from hounding him over past due taxes.

Louis had earned millions as a beloved champ, the first Black man since Jack Johnson to win boxing's world heavyweight title. He'd also spent, gambled, or just plain frittered away his fortune many times over, with Uncle Sam constantly picking through the lint in his pockets to find whatever might be left.

That tale of woe dampened few spirits in the opposing corner on Oct. 26, 1951 — 75 years ago Monday. The 28-year-old Rocky Marciano, who'd come into this fight as a betting underdog, was celebrating a victory over the man who'd once been his hero. His unbeaten record, so carefully maintained by his wily manager, remained intact. Back home in Brockton, Massachusetts, where they'd learned to always bet on the boy they knew as Rocco Marchegiano, they were counting their winnings and planning the victory parade, which would eventually include a cake 10-feet high.

But this wasn't even a title fight. For that, young Marciano would have to wait another year. But a knockout victory over the great Joe Louis was almost worth more. In the winner's locker room, manager Al Weill pointed at Marciano and said, "There stands 2 million bucks in cold cash."

Over in the other locker room, Louis was reckoning with a bleaker future. The ex-champ lay facedown on a massage table with one hand resting in a bucket of ice as he answered the newspapermen's questions. Yes, he told them, this Marciano kid hit hard. Yes, probably even harder than Max Schmeling, the only other fighter to ever knock Louis out. Then again, Louis said, he was 22 years old back when Schmeling got to him.

"You can take more then than later on," he said. He didn't have to tell any of the reporters that this, what they were witnessing now, was the last stop of the "later on" period.

"An old man's dream ended," Red Smith would write of the fight in the New York Herald Tribune. "A young man's vision of the future opened wide. Young men have visions, old men have dreams. But the place for old men to dream is beside the fire."

The story of how both men arrived at that intersection of boxing's past and future is a familiar one to any fight fan. It's the classic and also tragic tale of how the sport makes the young eat the old to secure their own place at the table. It's a story about what it meant — and what it was worth — to be a hero in post-war America. Even now, 75 years later, it remains a saga of hard triumphs and unpleasant realities. And still it has plenty to teach us about life in and out of the ring.

When he first won the heavyweight title in 1937, knocking out "The Cinderella Man" James J. Braddock at Chicago's Comiskey Park, Louis vowed to be "a fighting champion." He meant it.

His first year as champ, Louis defended the belt four times, culminating with a brutal first-round knockout of Schmeling to avenge his only professional loss. He would maintain that pace, notching four heavyweight title defenses per year, until 1941, when he somehow logged seven straight title defenses in one calendar year, a feat that will likely never be repeated. Before his reign was over, Louis would defend the heavyweight belt more than the previous nine champions combined.

That run was not without complications and criticisms. By the early 1940s, Louis had dispatched all serious contenders to the heavyweight throne. His management triad — Mike Jacobs, John Roxborough and Julian Black — kept him busy in order to keep the money faucet flowing. Sometimes that meant getting creative about his matchups, as when they tapped New Jersey bartender "Two Ton" Tony Galento to bring his colorful persona and bowling ball physique to Yankee Stadium for a shot at Louis' title.

But the press had begun calling Louis' steady stream of opponents the "Bum of the Month Club," and the box office returns were diminishing. After earning a purse of nearly $350,000 (about $8.3 million in 2026 dollars) for his rematch with Schmeling, his first five fights in 1941 brought in less than $120,000 combined. It didn't help that money seemed to flow through Louis' hands like water in a mountain stream.

In his exhaustive biography, "Joe Louis," Randy Roberts recounts a description of Louis' spending habits from lawyer and longtime friend Truman Gibson:

"The thing you have to understand about Joe is that he lived every day," Gibson said. "I went to school, I planned for the future, Joe Louis lived every day."

He kept apartments in Chicago and New York. He owned a sprawling horse ranch in Michigan. He had closets overflowing with expensive suits and he meticulously tracked what he wore so as not to be seen in the same outfit too many times. He handed money out freely to friends and strangers, and developed an almost pathological habit of gambling on his golf game. In an autobiography, Louis would recall how he'd started betting more and more heavily out on the links, "but damn, I was losing a lot of money."

One friend recalled that Louis would occasionally come home from losing large sums on the links and then break his own clubs in disgust and frustration, only to buy more later.

"He was like a man with alcohol," said his longtime friend Sunnie Wilson. "It was an addiction."

Louis' motivation to stay busy as champ was driven in part by his constant need to refill his coffers. But he was so far ahead of the pack as a fighter that finding him anyone who could put up enough of a fight to make for a good show only got more challenging. In 27 title fights between 1937 and 1948, only four opponents went the distance with Louis.

Louis' toughest test in the ring during this period came against light heavyweight champ Billy Conn, who moved up a division to challenge him in the summer of 1941. Conn was undersized, but a deft technician whose quickness proved frustrating for Louis, who had become used to being the faster man at heavyweight.

"He was like a mosquito," Louis said later. "He'd sting and move."

For the better part of 12 rounds, "The Pittsburgh Kid" picked Louis apart. His punches didn't seem to be damaging Louis, but he was clearly wearing the champion down and his confidence grew as the fight went on. In the 13th, Conn decided it was time to put Louis away. He knew he was ahead on the scorecards, but later explained that he believed the heavyweight title was something that should change hands via knockout — not via the judges.

This proved to be a grave mistake. Once Conn decided to stand and trade rather than hit and run, Louis began tagging him with hard shots. A Louis left hook late in the round, followed by a thudding right behind the ear, sent Conn tumbling down, his head bouncing violently off the canvas.

Conn rose slowly, appearing to stand just before referee Eddie Joseph reached a full 10-count. But one look in Conn's eyes and Joseph decided to wave it off. Conn offered no protest.

Asked later why he didn't just stay away from Louis for the final three rounds and win the title on points, Conn replied: "What's the sense of being Irish if you can't be dumb?"

The fight was such a dramatic sensation that a rematch seemed inevitable. Two things worked to prevent it. First, Conn broke his hand on his father-in-law's head during one of many arguments about whether he was good enough for the man's daughter, resulting in a delay. Then, on Dec. 7, 1941, Japan bombed Pearl Harbor. The United States was at war, and soon Joe Louis was too.

No one outside the working class manufacturing town of Brockton, Massachusetts, had ever heard of Rocco Marchegiano at the start of World War II. Just another kid from yet another family of Italian immigrants, he was 18 when the U.S. declared war on Japan and Germany. Like the other boys he'd grown up with, he was essentially just waiting for the inevitable draft notice.

That notice eventually arrived in 1943, leading to an entirely undistinguished career in the U.S. Army, except for one detail — it was where he first discovered boxing.

The boy who would later become Rocky Marciano had always been a sports fanatic. He'd grown up on the sandlots of Brockton's Ward 2, the son of Italian immigrants who, like most others in the neighborhood, made their living in the city's factories.

His father had come to America as a teenager, then enlisted in World War I, eager to fight for the adopted homeland he was so proud of. He'd been terribly wounded in battle, both by shrapnel and by the poison gas deployed by the Germans. He returned to work in a Brockton shoe factory after the war, but his body was shriveled and depleted by the toxins. It was said that, for the rest of his life, he always kept a hard candy in his mouth to drive out the lingering taste of the gas.

In the America of Marciano's youth, baseball was the pinnacle of the athletic world. As a stocky, muscular kid with thick legs and short arms, Marciano was a natural as a catcher. He made for a powerful hitter, but he was comically slow on the base path. An uncle had built him a homemade heavy bag, which young Rocco thumped on regularly, but his actual fighting experience was limited to neighborhood tussles, which were so frequent as to be mostly unremarkable.

He'd gotten a glimpse of professional boxing as a kid down at the Brockton Arena. According to Mike Stanton's excellent biography, "Unbeaten: Rocky Marciano's Fight for Perfection in a Crooked World," Rocco and friends would get into events for free by working odd jobs at the arena. At the height of the Great Depression, the promoter could afford only one set of gloves for the fighters, so Rocco and other kids would make themselves useful between bouts by quickly taking the gloves off one fighter and bringing them to the next man on the fight card so the event could proceed.

One night they even got to stand close to greatness, when heavyweight champion Joe Louis made an appearance at a Brockton boxing event. The starstruck young boys, Rocco among them, followed Louis everywhere — even to the bathroom. One friend of Marciano's recalled that Louis had been uncommonly patient with their invasions of his privacy, pressing 50 cents into each boy's hand as he left.

But Marciano didn't seriously lace up the gloves himself until the Army, and even then it was mostly to get out of other duties. He was not a good soldier by any metric. He chafed at the restrictions, at being constantly told what to do. But when his unit shipped out to the coastal city of Swansea, in the United Kingdom, it brought Marciano near enough to a real, working boxing gym run by a Welsh heavyweight named Jim Wilde.

Marciano learned the first inklings of boxing craft there, but he also landed himself in serious trouble. Along with another soldier, Marciano was accused of beating and robbing a British man after a night of heavy drinking. Both men denied the charges and claimed self-defense against homosexual "advances," but were swiftly convicted in a court martial.

While Marciano's unit headed to France to join the war, he sat in the brig, awaiting punishment. His commanding officer described the young private as "an unreliable and unsatisfactory soldier" whose prior offenses "have always been minor enough to avoid trial by court martial, but they have been consistent and numerous." He concluded that Marciano was "of no value to the Army."

Marciano's war record remained a well-kept secret during his later rise to fame. When asked by reporters, he would typically remain vague, saying he saw no combat heroics and was just another one of the boys over there doing what he could. This read as good-natured humility in the papers, but also concealed the fact that he'd spent nearly two years as a military prisoner before being reassigned to Fort Lewis, Washington, where he extended his military service — unpaid — in order to turn his dishonorable discharge into an honorable one.

Returning to Brockton after the war, Marciano was a high-school dropout whose dreams of a big-league baseball career were doomed by his slow legs. He'd learned to box in the Army, and had even logged some rough semblance of a few bouts with other soldiers. But it wasn't until a local promoter agreed to stick him in a fight for the sake of a hometown draw that he got a real taste of what boxing was like.

Technically, it was an amateur fight, though Marciano — then still going by his family name "Marchegiano" — mostly did it for the $30 fee he'd receive for "expenses." He'd always been known as a tough kid in the neighborhood, ready and willing to fight all comers, but he wasn't in great cardiovascular shape. That was before he stopped at his uncle's house on the way to the arena and ate a big plate of macaroni, which did him no favors.

His first opponent was an experienced amateur heavyweight named Henry Lester who easily evaded Marciano's wild swings. The neighborhood kid was a game brawler, which pleased the local crowd, but he wasn't much of a boxer. By the start of the second round, he was so exhausted that he could barely hold up his gloves. As Lester began pummeling him against the ropes, Marciano defended himself by kneeing Lester in the groin.

He was immediately disqualified. He would later claim it was an accident, but the referee that night remembered it differently.

"The kid just plain kneed him in the balls," he explained.

Marciano was embarrassed, saying later: "That was my first hometown fight and I lost it." He resolved to never again show up for a fight in anything less than stellar shape.

He mostly kept that promise to himself, becoming fanatical and even monastic about his training. Years later, deep in training camp while preparing to defend his heavyweight title, it was said he even rejected the advances of famous actress Jayne Mansfield (though it was also said that he made up for lost time after retiring).

Marciano believed, he said, that "you've got to make boxing a kind of religion. You believe in yourself and you believe in the things you got to do. You never forget them for a minute."

But early on, Marciano's future in boxing seemed limited. Just being a dreadfully slow runner had doomed his hopes of playing professional baseball, even after a tryout with the Chicago Cubs. His short arms and plodding movements didn't auger well for his hopes of turning into a successful heavyweight. Even as he gained experience and training, he still fought like a brawler. Early opponents found him easy to hit, though nearly impossible to actually hurt.

For those first few years as a pro, that was Marciano's saving grace. He couldn't box all that well. He wasn't especially clever as a fighter. At about 5-foot-10 and 185 pounds when he was in shape, he was undersized for the heavyweight division. But he could take anyone's best punch and keep coming forward. And once he inevitably got close enough to land his own shots, he hit like a train.

"I got a guy who's short, stoop-shouldered and balding with two left feet," trainer Charley Goodman once said. "They all look better than he does as far as the moves are concerned, but they don't look so good on the canvas."

Marciano's career began to get serious when he relocated to New York City and signed with manager Al Weill, a fast-talking, cigar-chomping wheeler and dealer who'd made the unlikely transition from competitive ballroom dancing to handling pro fighters. He had a reputation for penny-pinching and for exerting a domineering control over his fighters, while never losing sight of the main goal — stuffing his own pockets.

As one writer put it: "Boxing will never be the spiritual leader of sports. And Al Weill will never be the spiritual leader of boxing."

Weill could see that Marciano had several physical deficiencies in addition to his lack of general boxing skill, but he also saw the marketing potential in a heavyweight who could — and would — take a beating in order to deliver one-punch dynamite.

Weill shepherded Marciano toward the trainer Goodman, who helped turn some of Marciano's physical shortcomings into stylistic assets. The most successful innovation was in teaching Marciano to fight out of a low crouch, making him even shorter but also harder to hit for taller, longer fighters. As they reached down for the ducking, driving Marciano, he would advance into their chests, hammering with short, powerful punches from inside their preferred range.

The strategy worked well, especially against lower-level fighters. Weill was quick to see that Marciano's undefeated record (early semi-pro losses were kept off his record, aided by the change of name from Marchegiano to Marciano) was as important from a marketing perspective as his crowd-friendly, power-punching style. As Marciano climbed the ranks, Weill was often directly criticized for protecting a fighter still rough around the edges by booking him in nothing but easy fights.

Earl Lofquist, a writer with the Providence Journal, had covered many of Marciano's early pro fights in Rhode Island, where he fought almost exclusively for the first couple years of his pro career. He criticized Marciano as overrated, writing that his opponents were "slightly animated punching bags." His handlers stressed that he'd picked up boxing relatively late in life, having only learned the sport in earnest in the Army. This placated some critics, but only for a time.

"You'd think the guy was a fragile egg to be kept under glass the way his opponents ([Roland] LaStarza excepted) have been handpicked," Lofquist wrote. "Whether this has been for Marciano's good can be doubted. His improvement over the past year has been slight. But then he has not been fighting anybody from whom he could learn anything."

Marciano's streak of knockout victories, along with his undefeated record, garnered more and more attention. And the state of post-war heavyweight boxing in America was shaping up as the perfect environment for his particular brand of brawling. All he needed was the right opportunity against the right opponent to make a name for himself that would ring out all over the country. This is how the misfortunes of a once great champion became the lucky break Marciano needed, and just in time.

During World War II, Joe Louis had been a poster boy for the U.S. Army — literally . He appeared on recruitment posters as "Pvt. Joe Louis," brandishing a rifle and bayonet along with a quote promising victory to America "because we're on God's side."

For more than two years, the heavyweight champion's professional career was effectively on hold. Some of the fights he did have during the war, such as a 1942 bout against Buddy Baer, were essentially charity matches, with proceeds going to causes such as the Navy Relief Society. Louis was also instrumental in the Army's efforts to recruit more Black soldiers, and to sell the war effort itself to a community still suffering under brutal discrimination in most of the country.

A saying at the time held that Black Americans believed in two things: God and Joe Louis. Early in the war, he was a vital bridge between the military apparatus of the nation and the Black soldiers who would be called upon to serve in segregated units that endured much poorer conditions. During World War II, the U.S. Armed Forces were still so racially segregated that a wounded white soldier would not be given blood taken from a Black one, and vice versa.

Louis mainly served in the Special Services Division, traveling around for recruitment events and entertaining troops with boxing exhibitions. Behind the scenes, he worked to ease the path for other Black soldiers, including a young Jackie Robinson. Shortly before his release from the military in 1945, he was given an award citing his "incalculable contribution to the general morale" of troops.

But it didn't take long for Uncle Sam to forget Louis' contributions once the war was over. As the IRS began examining his tax returns, it found one reason after another to increase Louis' overall tax bill. Even some of the charity bouts, for which he profited hardly at all, came back to bite him at tax time.

It didn't help that Louis, who seemed to regard money as a thing that passed through his hands but was never fully owned by him, had already spent most of his earnings. The government kept adding to the tally, and the interest kept ticking the number up even higher. To get by, Louis was taking advances on future earnings from his managers, which placed him ever more firmly under their control.

By 1950, following audits of several years' past tax returns, the IRS assessed Louis' debt to the U.S. government at around $500,000 — the equivalent of around $7.1 million today. He owed money to his managers, as well as to his ex-wife Marva, toward whom he hardly even attempted to be faithful, and whom he would marry and divorce twice — once in 1945, and then again in 1949.

But even while he was successfully defending his heavyweight title, it became clear Louis' skills were in decline. He won successive bouts in 1947-48 against "Jersey" Joe Walcott, though unimpressively. After the second bout, he declared himself finished with fighting at the age of 34.

"That's my last fight," Louis said. "I've been around a long time and I think that it's about time to quit. And I'm glad to quit with the title still mine."

Retirement did not come easy. Louis was restless, sometimes taking off on a whim and staying gone for days or weeks. He struggled to find ways of making enough money to keep pace with his ballooning tax debt, plus what he owed to the managers who had been slipping him money while keep a careful accounting of what they expected to get back. In 1950, he announced a comeback against Ezzard Charles, who'd claimed the vacant title by beating Walcott after Louis did.

The fight was a sad affair. Louis looked slow and out of shape. He made it the distance, but the judges' decision for Charles was a formality.

A report on the fight in The New York Times concluded: "Everybody knew his reflexes must have suffered. That's inevitable. Few suspected his coordination would be what it was, so amazingly lacking that it was non-existent."

After the fight he again declared his retirement. "I'll never fight again," Louis told reporters. "Positively."

But he did, of course. Just two months later. He had to. It was the only hope he had of earning enough money to be free of his debtors — both public and private — even though the returns on his bouts were getting smaller and smaller.

Louis' heyday as champ had come in the age of radio. Millions of Americans listened to the play-by-play of his fights broadcast over the airwaves in the 1930s, but to see his boxing beauty and brilliance for themselves they had to buy a ticket.

In post-war America, the television was rapidly replacing radio as the primary means of home entertainment. Between the end of World War II and the early 1950s, television ownership in America had grown from a few thousand sets to around 12 million. This changed the economic realities for boxing , and those who tuned in to see their hero Louis often wound up disappointed by his obvious signs of aging.

Still, even a Louis in decline was good enough to beat most heavyweights of the era. After the title fight loss to Charles, he reeled off eight straight wins, though knockout victories were now in shorter supply. There was even talk that he might manage to work his way back to the heavyweight championship. For that, he'd need an eye-catching win. The young, undefeated Marciano seemed to be the only option who would fit the bill.

Some in Marciano's camp questioned the wisdom of the match. Wasn't Louis exactly the kind of fighter Marciano should avoid? He had technique but also size and power. If Marciano was really a paper tiger, Louis could expose him. It didn't help that, either due to his own dire financial condition or his well-known dislike and distrust for Marciano's manager Weill, Louis had insisted on an uncommonly uneven cut for the proceeds of the fight. Louis would fight Marciano only if he received 45% of the money, leaving just 15% for the unbeaten youngster. Weill advised Marciano to take it anyway.

"Old guys like Louis go all of a sudden," Weill said. "If we don't get him first, someone else will."

The fight was originally set for Manhattan's Polo Grounds, but was moved to Madison Square Garden after Bobby Thompson hit the "shot heard round the world" to keep the New York Giants' season going with a National League pennant win in early October.

By the day of the fight on Oct. 26, 1951, Louis vs. Marciano had captured imaginations all over America. It was an especially hot ticket in Brockton, where a special ticket office had been opened to capitalize on Marciano's hometown fame. By this point, he was more than a hero to the people there — he was a cash cow. The people of Brockton were known for betting everything from the rent to the grocery money on their man.

"They couldn't afford to see me lose," Marciano said of his supporters in Brockton. "I always knew I would get up."

But this time Marciano was the underdog. He had power, yes. His right hand had snapped off the front teeth of a recent opponent at the gums. But could he get close enough to land that punch on a savvy fighter like the former champ? Louis didn't seem to think so. He told reporters that he'd gone to watch film of Marciano's fight with Rex Layne, which took place earlier that same year, and had walked out of the theater.

When told of this, Marciano said he didn't blame Louis for walking out. He hadn't fought well that night. But he knew he could do better. He was also, despite the press and the attention and the stakes, seemingly unconcerned. As one trainer said of him, "He goes in for a fight like I go in for a glass of beer."

Walking into Madison Square Garden that night, Marciano was walking into enemy territory. He had a vocal cheering section of a few thousand fans from Brockton, but the rest of the crowd seemed to be in the Louis camp.

The famed boxing writer A.J. Liebling, writing about the fight in his classic boxing book "The Sweet Science," recalled that Louis had somehow looked younger than his 37 years while walking around in street clothes, with a hat that "hid the bald spot." But on fight night the bald spot and the softening midsection were on full display.

"It's when he gets into a ring that age comes on him," Liebling wrote of Louis.

Any doubts about Marciano's ability to get close enough to hurt Louis were put to rest in the first round. He charged across the ring at the older man, bullying him back toward the ropes with his head in the former champ's chest. Liebling wrote that Marciano's right hand had "received all the advance publicity," but it was the left that wound up hurting Louis more in the fight.

"The way I figured it, Louis was being so careful about that crazy Marciano right that he was afraid to pull his own left back to hook," Liebling wrote. "He would just jab and drop his forearm onto Rocky's right biceps, so he couldn't counter. Sooner or later, Joe would throw the hook, I thought, and that would end the fight. It looked like a fight between two men with one good hand apiece."

Louis did throw the left, and even landed cleanly with it. It was the same punch he'd used to drop so many opponents during his championship prime. But Marciano seemed entirely unbothered by it. He kept pressing forward, and late in the opening round landed a solid shot that wobbled Louis.

"I think that punch was the one that made Joe feel old," Liebling wrote.

Then, in the middle rounds, Louis began to show signs of a revival. The jab came back to life. He seemed to be winning rounds. Maybe he couldn't hurt Marciano, but he could hit him and he could wear him down. He just had to stay mobile enough to avoid that right hand.

But in the eighth, Marciano proved he did in fact have two good hands. One leaping left hook was all it took to sit Louis down in the corner. He rose quickly to one knee, then waited for his head to clear. Once he rose to his feet, Marciano swarmed him. As Louis tried to tie his arms up, Marciano fired off short hooks and uppercuts, nothing but power shots, with more coming all the time, even if he missed with half of them.

A slicing left came up almost from the floor and knocked Louis against the ropes, his legs trembling involuntarily. Marciano followed up with the same punch again, and now Louis' hands began to sink down toward his sides. He might have fallen right there if Marciano had stepped back and let him.

Instead, the young contender uncorked that dreaded right hand on a now defenseless Louis, knocking him through the ropes and onto the ring apron.

A count was unnecessary. The focus now was on helping Louis back into the ring, back to his feet, where he could congratulate the coming man of the division.

"I remember looking out at the crowd and how everyone just sat there in silence," Marciano recalled later. "Only the guys from my hometown in Brockton were making any noise."

Once Louis was upright again, Marciano went over and offered his apologies.

"You don't have to be sorry," Louis is said to have told him. "You licked me fair and square."

Back in his office a couple weeks later, Weill couldn't stop gloating. He'd accurately assessed the situation for what it was, and now he and Marciano stood to make boatloads of cash from the fame that came with being only the second man to ever knock out Joe Louis.

"What did I tell you?" Weill said to Liebling. "You want to look out for them broken fighters."

Louis was finally finished with boxing. He meant it this time. He never fought another professional match, though he did keep a hand in various forms of fight sports purely for the money. For a time he even worked as a professional wrestler. When asked if that wasn't a humiliating vocation for the former heavyweight champ, he replied only that it "beats stealing."

Not everyone could stomach seeing Louis in a wrestling ring. His second wife (but third marriage), Rose Morgan, was always against it.

"To me, Joe Louis was like the President of the United States," she told a reporter. "How would you like to see the President of the United States washing dishes? That's how I felt about Joe wrestling."

An accidental injury forced him out of the field soon enough, though he would occasionally work matches as a referee. He still owed an astounding tax debt, and would ultimately die still under that burden.

"I owe the government well over $1,000,000 in back taxes," he said in the late 1950s. "I don't actually know how much the total is, and I don't think the government does either."

But the government did know. The debt was around $2 million when Louis died in 1981. In his later years, some of Louis' behavior became increasingly erratic and worrisome to those around him. He began using drugs like heroin, which he initially blamed on a woman who he claimed had administered the drug while he was sleeping. He also used cocaine, and seemed to go through bouts of extreme paranoia.

When he checked into hotels, he would tape cardboard over the vents and smear mayonnaise on the ceiling, which he said was to prevent poison gas from seeping into his room. He sometimes thought he was being tailed by hired killers, occasionally threatening strangers whom he thought were following him. In 1970, his fourth wife, Martha Jefferson, had him committed to a hospital for psychiatric evaluation. Every day she visited and brought him fruit, which Louis would distribute to the other patients.

Louis spent most of his later years in Las Vegas, working as a casino greeter at Caesar's Palace. Gregarious and instantly recognizable, he was well-suited to the role. The casino would give him a pocketful of chips and he would happily gamble them away, which in turn encouraged other patrons to throw their money down right beside them, just so they could tell their friends back home how they had once shot dice with Joe Louis.

His old foe Billy Conn recalled visiting him in Las Vegas and watching as Louis gave a chip worth $100 to a man begging for change. When Conn pointed out that he also had $25 chips and could have easily handed the man that one instead, Louis shrugged.

"What the hell's the difference?" he said. "I'm going to lose it anyway."

While he certainly felt the stress of his debts, Louis never seemed to grow bitter about the relentless hounding from the same government he once so eagerly served. He also refused to complain about life in the ring, or how earnings for boxers skyrocketed only after his time was done.

"I ain't sorry I fought when I did," he said. "In my time, I made $5,000,000, wound up broke, and owe the government $1,000,000 in taxes. If I was fighting today, I'd earn $10,000,000, would still wind up broke, and would owe the government $2,000,000."

He did, of course, owe the government that sum when he died. Still, to observers he seemed to be a man with few regrets. Biographer Randy Roberts wrote that, by the time Louis retired for good at the age of 37, he was worse off in many ways than before the first time he slipped on a pair of boxing gloves.

"Then, he had nothing," Roberts wrote. "Now, he had much less. In between he had it all."

Marciano, of course, went on to become the world heavyweight champion with a 1952 knockout of "Jersey" Joe Walcott. He defended the belt six times, retiring after his knockout of Archie Moore at Yankee Stadium in 1955. He became the rare heavyweight champion to walk away from the sport undefeated and actually stay that way. He faced his own struggles with retired life, overindulging his appetites for both food and women. He was also restless, traveling often, and hoarding cash in strange places, all due to a constant fear of losing it all.

Even after retiring with a perfect 49-0 professional record, some critics still maintained that he was overrated. He'd come along at a particularly weak time for the heavyweight division, they said, then got out before the talent improved.

Arthur Daley, of The New York Times, once observed that "no man reached the championship with more physical handicaps" than Marciano, but also noted, amid comparisons to boxing's prior greats, that "if Marciano is the second Jack Dempsey, the first Jack Dempsey should sue him for libel."

Marciano ultimately died in a plane crash the day before his 46th birthday. He was a passenger in a small Cessna plane, flying from Chicago to Des Moines, Iowa, where he had agreed to make an appearance at a restaurant. The pilot, who had limited experience flying at night, became disoriented in a fog bank. Reports later said there was only one tree in the field where he tried to set the plane down, and they had hit it.

"Start the count, he'll get up," the great Los Angeles Times sportswriter Jim Murray wrote after news spread of Marciano's death on Aug. 31, 1969. "A lot of us today are wishing there were an honest referee in a cornfield in Iowa."

Marciano remains the only man to retire undefeated as boxing's heavyweight champion. There are still those who debate where he belongs in the all-time rankings, and whether it is truly ahead of Louis, who held the title for so long, defeated so many, and might have added even more triumphs to his tally if not for the outbreak of World War II. Just because Marciano beat him in his waning years, does that really make him the better heavyweight? It's an argument for barbershops to this day.

One thing that's less debatable about Marciano is how much he made of his career despite what would seem to be major deficiencies. Even at the time, this perplexed onlookers.

Liebling later told a story of being baffled as to the approach Ezzard Charles took in his bouts with Marciano. Why didn't he fight more aggressively? Why did he seem so content to be counted out after being dropped by the champ in their rematch? It wasn't until he pressed boxing trainer Freddie Brown on the question that he got his answer.

"He fought the way he fought because Marciano fought the way he fought," Brown explained. " … It is not like football. Rocky never gives you the ball."

articles.title: Paul Smith: Fighters are being 'exploited and forgotten' in a failing system, says former boxer
articles.summary: Fighters are being "hurt, exploited or forgotten" in a failing system, says former boxer Paul Smith, who has criticised a lack of support for athletes.
articles.body:
Fighters are being "hurt, exploited or forgotten" in a failing system, says former boxer Paul Smith, who has criticised a lack of support for athletes.

Smith is part of a team set up to represent fighters and safeguard their futures, with the group aiming to launch the "biggest ever inquiry into health and safety in combat sport".

The group, called the Global Fighters' Association (GFA), wants the inquiry to provide the platform for it to become "the new umbrella organisation for all combat sport".

It was set up last year with the aim of creating a union to safeguard fighters' futures.

The GFA says it wants to campaign for fair contracts and better pay, insurance and pensions, proper health and safety standards and somewhere for fighters to report problems to an official channel.

It points to public fundraisers in recent months which have helped fighters such as Lee Reeves pay for emergency care after serious injuries.

Smith, who challenged three times for a super-middleweight world title before his retirement in 2017, says it is a "failing" of the system when fighters like Reeves have to raise money to pay for recovery.

"Every week, somewhere in this sport, a fighter is hurt, exploited or forgotten, and the only safety net is whatever the boxing community can scrape together after the fact," said Smith.

"That's not a system. That's a failing. We are not aware of anyone, ever, who has properly invested the time and resources to get under the bonnet of this sport, work out exactly where it is failing fighters, and publish actionable recommendations to fix it."

The GFA says it has secured respected barrister Jonathan Caplan KC to lead the process of conducting the inquiry, which will look into the "safety, governance and treatment of combat sports participants at all levels", from grassroots to professional.

He will be tasked with producing a report back on the evidence and testimonies gathered.

The GFA is a non-profit organisation and is aiming to raise £500,000 to fund the inquiry via a crowdfunding campaign.

Chair designate Simon Bazalgette says the group wants to provide fighters with the same support available to athletes in other sports.

"Over the last decade or so, professional sports such as rugby, football and horse racing have raised their game when it comes to the welfare of the participants," said Bazalgette.

"It is striking that combat sport is one of the last workplaces with no professional representation for its workers, meaning little protection, no minimum health and safety standard, no independent pension scheme, no insurance floor, and no single body a fighter can turn to when something goes wrong.

"The GFA has been formed to rectify this, to help the sport create a stronger bond of trust with its participants and its audience, and thereby give a stronger foundation for growth."

Earlier this month, British mixed martial arts (MMA) fighter Michael 'Venom' Page urged fighters to form a union to campaign for better pay.

He pointed to the Muhammad Ali Act - a 2000 US law designed to protect boxers' rights and combat potential monopolies - as something he would like to replicate in MMA.

UFC president Dana White has been spearheading a push to amend the act - a move which GFA acting general secretary Paul Maloney says should cause alarm bells in fighters.

"It's the one piece of legislation anywhere in the world that gives fighters a level of workplace protection, and it's currently being rewritten in a way critics say favours the promoters and networks that already hold most of the power," said Maloney.

"If it can be stripped back there, it can happen anywhere else that lacks its own independent, respected voice for fighters - which is exactly why the GFA exists."

articles.title: Governo restabelece regras e libera pesca na foz do Rio Doce  | G1
articles.standfirst: Atividade estava proibida desde 2016; segundo especialistas ouvidos pelo g1, liberação foi baseada em nota técnica da Anvisa sobre a segurança do consumo de pescado, com dados de monitoramento da Ufes.
articles.summary: Atividade estava proibida desde 2016; segundo especialistas ouvidos pelo g1, liberação foi baseada em nota técnica da Anvisa sobre a segurança do consumo de pescado.
articles.body:
Após 10 anos, o governo federal publicou uma portaria que restabelece as regras e libera as atividades pesqueiras na área marinha próxima à foz do Rio Doce, entre Aracruz e Linhares , no Espírito Santo. Confira a publicação aqui.

A pesca na região estava proibida desde 2016, após uma decisão judicial relacionada aos riscos de contaminação provocados pelo rompimento da barragem de Fundão, em Mariana (MG).

Segundo especialistas ouvidos pelo g1 , a liberação foi baseada em uma nota técnica da Agência Nacional de Vigilância Sanitária (Anvisa), que apontou segurança para o consumo do pescado da região a partir de dados de monitoramento realizados pela Universidade Federal do Espírito Santo (Ufes).

Com a publicação da Portaria Interministerial MPA/MMA nº 75, as normas que regulamentavam a pesca antes da proibição voltam a valer.

Especial desastre de Mariana 1 ano depois: barco navega na foz do Rio Doce em novembro de 2015 — Foto: Flávia Mantovani/G1

A medida não cria novas regras, mas restabelece as que já disciplinavam a atividade, incluindo modalidades de pesca, equipamentos permitidos, espécies que podem ser capturadas e períodos de defeso, quando a pesca é suspensa para proteger a reprodução dos animais.

A área abrangida pela portaria vai de Barra do Riacho, em Aracruz, até Degredo/Ipiranguinha, em Linhares, em uma faixa marítima de até 20 metros de profundidade.

A norma também prevê o monitoramento da atividade pesqueira e determina que eventuais decisões sobre abertura, suspensão ou fechamento da pesca considerem dados atualizados, relatórios e publicações científicas.

Em nota, os Ministérios da Pesca e Aquicultura (MPA) e do Meio Ambiente e Mudança do Clima (MMA) informaram que a retomada será acompanhada por um plano integrado de monitoramento e avaliação, que poderá ser atualizado conforme novos dados científicos e a participação das comunidades pesqueiras.

Ainda conforme a ata, as regras poderão ser revistas ou suspensas a qualquer momento , conforme os resultados do monitoramento.

A medida não altera o pagamento do Programa de Transferência de Renda (PTR) nem substitui as obrigações de reparação relacionadas ao rompimento da barragem.

O g1 também acionou o Ministério Público Federal (MPF) e aguarda posicionamento.

Questionado sobre a qualidade da água, o Ministério da Saúde informou ao g1 que, com a Agência Brasileira de Apoio à Gestão do SUS (AgSUS), coordena o Programa Especial de Saúde do Rio Doce (PES Rio Doce) voltado à reparação em saúde das populações atingidas pelo rompimento da barragem de Fundão.

Informou em nota que o monitoramento da água é realizado pela AgSUS, enquanto a Funasa e laboratórios terceirizados realizam as análises.

Os resultados são encaminhados às vigilâncias estaduais e municipais, responsáveis, em conjunto com as demais instâncias competentes, pela adoção das medidas necessárias. Os estudos para avaliar os impactos à saúde serão desenvolvidos pela Rede de Pesquisas em Saúde do Rio Doce, coordenada pela Fiocruz.

Na análise realizada em julho, todas as fontes de água dos municípios de Colatina e Baixo Guandu apresentaram resultados dentro dos padrões de potabilidade. Esse índice foi de 90% em Linhares, 87% em Sooretama, 73% em Aracruz, 67% em São Mateus e 50% em Marilândia. Entre as formas de abastecimento monitoradas, estão água encanada, poços artesianos e cisternas familiares.

Em fevereiro de 2016, a Justiça Federal do Espírito Santo concedeu uma liminar que proibiu, por tempo indeterminado, a pesca de qualquer natureza na foz do Rio Doce, com exceção da atividade destinada à pesquisa científica.

Na época, a decisão atendeu a um pedido do Ministério Público Federal (MPF), que apontou a falta de estudos conclusivos sobre a contaminação de peixes, moluscos e crustáceos que vivem na região após a chegada dos rejeitos da barragem de Fundão, rompida em novembro de 2015.

A preocupação era tanto com os possíveis riscos à saúde de quem consumisse o pescado quanto com os impactos sobre o ecossistema marinho.

articles.title: WWE, ante una decisión de alto riesgo: Crown Jewel, en el aire por la guerra en Arabia Saudí
articles.standfirst: La compañía sigue adelante con los planes de viaje
articles.summary: La compañía sigue adelante con los planes de viaje
articles.body: La escalada de violencia en Oriente Medio pone contra las cuerdas los planes de WWE para el próximo 7 de noviembre. Riad tiene previsto acoger una nueva edición de Crown Jewel, uno de los grandes eventos que la compañía mantiene en su calendario internacional por contrato, pero el escenario geopolítico amenaza con convertir la cita en un problema que va mucho más allá del espectáculo. Con ataques con misiles y drones, aeropuertos afectados y advertencias oficiales sobre los riesgos para la seguridad, viajar a Arabia Saudí empieza a plantear una pregunta incómoda: ¿merece la pena asumir semejante exposición para celebrar un evento de lucha libre? La situación ha dado un giro especialmente delicado después de que el Departamento de Estado de Estados Unidos ordenara, el pasado 23 de octubre, la salida de Arabia Saudí de los empleados gubernamentales y de sus familiares que no desempeñan funciones de emergencia. Una recomendación que adquiere una dimensión todavía mayor cuando se pone en perspectiva con los problemas que están sufriendo las infraestructuras aeroportuarias del país. Y es que el riesgo no se limita a una zona concreta ni a las consecuencias indirectas del conflicto. Las autoridades estadounidenses advierten de ataques contra aeropuertos civiles y otras infraestructuras críticas, así como de posibles cierres del espacio aéreo, cancelaciones y graves interrupciones en los desplazamientos. El aeropuerto internacional Rey Khalid de Riad ha anunciado una reapertura parcial, mientras que las instalaciones de Yeda y Dammam continúan registrando retrasos y cancelaciones. En este contexto, la posibilidad de que cientos de trabajadores, luchadores, técnicos, responsables de producción y miembros de los equipos de retransmisión de WWE tengan que desplazarse hasta territorio saudí obliga a mirar el calendario con otros ojos. No se trata únicamente de organizar un espectáculo de primer nivel: también está en juego la seguridad de todas las personas que hacen posible el evento. Por ahora, WWE sigue teniendo Crown Jewel en su horizonte. En los últimos programas semanales se han escuchado referencias al evento en distintas promociones, aunque sin hacer especial hincapié en su localización. Ese detalle alimenta las dudas, pero no permite concluir que la compañía esté preparando un cambio de sede o que haya decidido cancelar el viaje. Mientras desde Arabia se sigue promocionando el evento, hay quien dice que WWE prepara Los Ángeles como sede alternativa para la celebración del PLE; eso sí cambiar de ubicación a última hora sería un desafío organizativo y económico, pero mantener los planes sin evaluar adecuadamente la situación de seguridad también podría tener consecuencias mucho más graves. Arabia Saudí se ha convertido en una pieza importante de la estrategia internacional de WWE. Lo que en sus primeros años generó controversia por las críticas relacionadas con los derechos humanos y las condiciones impuestas a las luchadoras fue dando paso a una relación comercial cada vez más normalizada. Sin embargo, el escenario actual introduce una variable de otra naturaleza: la amenaza directa derivada de un conflicto armado y sus posibles repercusiones sobre el transporte y la seguridad de los asistentes. Mientras la incertidumbre crece fuera del cuadrilátero, WWE ya tiene varios combates anunciados para la velada. El cartel incluye enfrentamientos de enorme atractivo para los aficionados, con algunos de los nombres más importantes de la compañía. Roman Reigns vs. Sami Zayn: un duelo anunciado entre los campeones mundiales de WWE. Liv Morgan vs. Chelsea Green: un enfrentamiento entre las campeonas femeninas de la compañía. Cody Rhodes vs. Randy Orton: un combate Last Man Standing, una de las estipulaciones más exigentes y espectaculares de la lucha libre. The Visión vs. Penta & Je’Von Evans. Campeonato Mundial por Parejas. Sobre el papel, Crown Jewel reúne argumentos para convertirse en una de las citas destacadas del calendario. Pero el atractivo deportivo queda inevitablemente condicionado por las circunstancias que rodean al evento. La cuestión ya no es únicamente si WWE podrá cumplir con sus compromisos comerciales en Riad. La pregunta es si existen garantías suficientes para trasladar hasta allí a todo el personal necesario en unas condiciones razonables de seguridad. La reapertura parcial de un aeropuerto no equivale, por sí sola, a la desaparición del riesgo, especialmente cuando las propias autoridades recomiendan extremar las precauciones. WWE todavía tiene que aclarar públicamente qué ocurrirá con Crown Jewel si la situación continúa deteriorándose. Una posible reubicación, un aplazamiento o el mantenimiento de los planes son escenarios distintos, con implicaciones logísticas y contractuales que la compañía tendría que valorar. Por ahora, no hay que confundir las advertencias oficiales con una confirmación de que el evento vaya a cancelarse ni dar por hecho que Riad será necesariamente atacada durante las fechas previstas. Pero tampoco sería prudente minimizar unas señales de alarma que afectan directamente a la aviación y a las infraestructuras civiles. El próximo 7 de noviembre, WWE quiere que todas las miradas estén puestas en el cuadrilátero. Sin embargo, la evolución de la guerra puede terminar imponiendo una realidad mucho más importante que cualquier rivalidad o campeonato. Porque, cuando un evento deportivo obliga a desplazar a cientos de profesionales a una zona sometida a advertencias de seguridad y con incidencias aeroportuarias, la prioridad debe ser clara: garantizar que el espectáculo no se celebre a costa de poner vidas en peligro.

articles.title: Conor Benn Calls Out Conor McGregor for 2027 Fight, Manny Pacquiao Reportedly on Rumored Wish List
articles.summary: Conor Benn is shooting for the stars as he considers his options for his return to the boxing ring.
articles.body:
Conor Benn is shooting for the stars as he considers his options for his return to the boxing ring.

Benn took to his Instagram story to repost a mock fight poster of him and UFC star Conor McGregor, adding the caption, "Any day of the week."

Volkanovski breaks record after title win at UFC 333

McGregor isn't the only big name Benn is targeting, as ESPN's James Regan reported that a source said boxing legend Manny Pacquiao is "also understood to be on Benn's wish list."

Benn is coming off a second-round knockout loss to Ryan Garcia in September. The source told Regan that the 30-year-old "expects to fight again in the early part of 2027 and wants a big-name opponent rather than a more low-key comeback bout."

McGregor has one fight left on his deal with the UFC, which is under the same TKO banner as Zuffa Boxing, where Benn is signed for four more fights. The Irishman is currently recovering from a torn meniscus and ACL injury suffered in his long-awaited UFC return fight against Max Holloway in July.

If Benn isn't able to land a fight against McGregor or Pacquiao, Regan noted that his former promoter, Eddie Hearn, has "teased a potential trilogy fight against Chris Eubank Jr." The two Brits fought twice in 2025 in front of sold-out crowds at Tottenham Hotspur Stadium, earning one win apiece.

articles.title: Amir Khan backs new inquiry to improve welfare, health and safety in boxing
articles.summary: Boxing lags behind other sports in welfare and safety standards; leading UK King’s Counsel launches inquiry to improve standards across boxing and combat sports; Global Fighters Association aims to establish boxing’s first trade union
articles.body:
Khan is one of Britain's most decorated boxers who won multiple world championship belts across several weights.

He has backed the Global Fighters Association's (GFA) appointment of leading UK barrister Jonathan Caplan KC to lead a "root-and-branch" inquiry into the safety, governance and treatment of boxers at every level of the sport.

Jonathan Caplan KC has been tasked with leading an inquiry to gather evidence from within boxing and other combat sports in order to raise standards around welfare, health and safety and governance issues.

He intends to consult a broad range of stakeholders, including fighters, coaches, physiotherapists, doctors, surgeons, referees, judges, promoters, boards of control, governing bodies, media commentators, venue operators, managers, and the friends and families of fighters.

Caplan, speaking to Sky Sports said: "We will publish I hope far-reaching recommendations explaining our conclusions.

"We're doing this inquiry late, it should have been done a long time ago.

"There have been other significant inquiries into sport. An MP-led select committee held an inquiry into concussion in sport around two years ago, while the Whyte Review examined allegations of physical and emotional abuse in British Gymnastics. Combat sports are now crying out for the same level of detailed scrutiny. The welfare of participants across all combat sports must be fundamental to what we're trying to achieve. This inquiry is long overdue, and it's something that has never been done before."

The inquiry has been commissioned by the Global Fighters Association (GFA), which aims to establish itself as the first trade union representing boxers and participants across other combat sports.

The GFA's goal is to become a collective voice for everyone involved in combat sports, from those training and competing at their local gym to professional athletes who depend on the sport for their livelihood. Its ambition is to represent participants at every level, both inside and outside the ring.

While the sport's biggest stars generate a significant proportion of its revenue, for every global superstar such as Anthony Joshua or Tyson Fury, there are hundreds of fighters further down the ladder working hard to make a living from the sport. Their welfare, financial security and long-term health are among the issues the inquiry aims to address.

Paul Smith enjoyed a professional boxing career spanning 2003 to 2017, competing at middleweight and super-middleweight. During that time, he won both English and British titles and challenged for a world title on three occasions.

Now a trainer and co-founder of the GFA, Smith told Sky Sports : "The average fighter going to work every day is just trying to make a living from professional boxing. There is enough money in the sport for them to earn a living, but at the moment, it's simply not reaching those fighters.

"There isn't a system in place that adequately protects fighters when it comes to health and safety. We've seen so many people injured in the ring and, unfortunately, boxing isn't a sport where you simply lose a race. You can suffer serious injuries, be hit and even be killed. As sad as it is, it happens."

Smith added: "We want to establish a union where fighters feel safe and know they have someone on their side. If something goes wrong, they should be able to pick up the phone and speak to someone who can support them straight away.

"There are so many situations where rules may have been breached and a fighter is required to attend a hearing or answer questions. We want a GFA representative to be there alongside them, ensuring they have support and someone looking after their interests. The same applies if they have a disagreement with their manager or become involved in a dispute."

The GFA says that, in recent months, several fighters have suffered serious injuries in and around the ring, leaving their families to rely on public fundraising pages and the goodwill of fellow fighters and promoters to cover emergency medical treatment and rehabilitation costs. The association argues that these cases highlight the need for a more robust, sport-wide system of protection and support for fighters.

Former world champion Amir Khan also voiced his support for the initiative, saying: "There has to be an organisation that sits above everything, somewhere we can all turn to when something goes wrong, whether it's in training, at a weigh-in, with a contract or even in retirement. The GFA is that organisation."

Founded in 2022, the Global Fighters Association (GFA) is stepping up its efforts to improve welfare and safety across boxing and other combat sports, with its ambitions now extending beyond a group of former fighters campaigning for change.

The association's chair-designate is Simon Bazalgette, former chief executive of the Jockey Club and an independent non-executive director of the English Football League (EFL). His experience across professional sport brings an additional perspective to the GFA's mission.

Bazalgette said: "Over the last decade or so, professional sports such as rugby, football and horse racing have raised their game when it comes to the welfare of the participants."

"They recognise that the brand of the sport increasingly depends on demonstrating that best-in-class welfare underpins any aspiration to grow the audience and the commercial value of the sport.

"It is striking that combat sport is one of the last workplaces with no professional representation for its workers, meaning little protection, no minimum health and safety standard, no independent pension scheme, no insurance floor, and no single body a fighter can turn to when something goes wrong."

When will the inquiry report its findings?

Jonathan Caplan KC confirmed he intends to conduct several inquiries, with the first focusing on health and safety in boxing and other combat sports. He hopes to publish the initial report by spring 2027.

Speaking to Sky Sports , Caplan said he would examine how other sports have approached similar challenges and consider the lessons that could be applied to combat sports.

"I'm certainly very interested in looking at comparative sports, the conclusions they've reached and the regulatory overviews that have been carried out.

"For example, a DCMS select committee inquiry into concussion in sport is going to be of great interest to me. I'll be looking at what's already been done elsewhere and, where it's relevant, we want to learn from it and apply those lessons."

Caplan stressed that the inquiry would be evidence-led, with fighters and their families contributing first-hand accounts to help inform its findings and recommendations.

"The whole purpose is to produce a comprehensive and reasoned report. We'll be speaking to fighters and their families to gather case studies. Those who choose not to follow the proposals we put forward will have to explain why, particularly if the evidence supports them.

"I suspect the evidence is going to point to quite a lot of innovations that are necessary and long overdue. I don't think anybody wants to see those recommendations ignored, and I don't think anyone wants to be the person who fails to act on sensible recommendations."

articles.title: Doble atropello mortal del exboxeador puertorriqueño Carlos 'El Topo' Gerena
articles.standfirst: Fue olímpico en Barcelona 1992 y llegó a disputar dos veces el título superpluma del CMB en 1998 y 1999
articles.summary: Fue olímpico en Barcelona 1992 y llegó a disputar dos veces el título superpluma del CMB en 1998 y 1999
articles.body: El exboxeador puertorriqueño Carlos 'El Topo' Gerena, quien representó a Puerto Rico en los Juegos Olímpicos de Barcelona 1992, murió a los 55 años tras ser atropellado en una carretera de Bayamón, su municipio natal, ubicado en el área metropolitana de la isla. La Policía de Puerto Rico identificó este martes como Gerena al peatón fallecido el lunes cuando fue impactado por un vehículo en la carretera PR-2. Posteriormente, otro vehículo que transitaba por la misma carretera, no se percató presuntamente de la presencia del cuerpo sobre el pavimento y lo arrolló nuevamente. El caso es investigado por la División de Homicidios de Bayamón, pueblo en el que ocurrió el fatal accidente y donde nació el expúgil en 1971. Gerena conquistó la medalla de bronce en el Mundial Juvenil de 1989 y la de plata en el peso gallo de los Juegos Panamericanos de La Habana en 1991. En los Juegos de Barcelona 1992 participó en el peso pluma (-57 kilos), superando la ronda inicial ante el indio Narendar Bisth Singh y cayendo en octavos frente al argelino Hocine Soltani, que finalmente sería bronce. Debutó como profesional en 1993 y totalizó 44 combates con marca de 38-6 con 30 KOs. Llegó a disputar dos veces el título superpluma del CMB en 1998 y 1999. Entre sus rivales más destacados cabe mencionar a Genaro 'Chicanito' Hernández, Jesús Chávez y Floyd Mayweather Jr. Su último combate fue en 2003. La Organización Mundial de Boxeo (OMB), con sede en Puerto Rico, lamentó este martes el fallecimiento de Gerena, expresando sus condolencias a su familia, amigos y a toda la comunidad boxística. En un mensaje en redes sociales, la OMB le describió como "una figura respetada del boxeo puertorriqueño cuya pasión y dedicación dejaron una huella duradera en este deporte".

articles.title: La redención de Yaman 'El Diamante': "Sé a lo que aspiro y a dónde voy a llegar"
articles.standfirst: El peleador de Mondragón habló con MARCA tras noquear a Ubay González en WOW 33 Vitoria
articles.summary: El peleador de Mondragón habló con MARCA tras noquear a Ubay González en WOW 33 Vitoria
articles.body: El WOW 33 celebrado en Vitoria el pasado sábado tuvo bastantes momentos destacados, pero sin duda uno de los más importantes fue la redención de Yaman 'El Diamante' (4-2) tras noquear a Ubay González (4-4) en el segundo asalto. El peleador de Mondragón venía de dos derrotas consecutivas, y habló con MARCA tras dar un golpe sobre la mesa para dejar una bonita reflexión de lo que supone para él este triunfo. "Me siento súper feliz, que algo que llevo trabajando durante tanto tiempo, y encima dadas las circunstancias, se refleje así. Lo dije en la previa, no voy a buscar nada, voy a fluir, quiero que todo llegue a mí. De repente coloqué la mano y se apagaron las luces", confesaba Yaman respecto a un K.O. que le permitió además llevarse el bono de 3.000 euros. Además, dejó una bonita reflexión, reconociendo que "ha sido el resultado de trabajar incansablemente, de aferrarme a mi sueño y de recuperar mi luz en la oscuridad. Al fin y al cabo, ¿cuándo necesitamos luz? Cuando estamos en la oscuridad. Sin la oscuridad, la luz no es necesaria. Siempre he tenido esa capacidad de que algo malo lo convierta en algo bueno. Así que, gracias a Dios hemos conseguido la victoria y un K.O. increíble". De hecho, ningún combate profesional de 'El Diamante' ha ido a los puntos. No hay que olvidar que Yaman tenía toda la presión sobre sus hombros, algo que no le pesó en ningún momento. "Me he sentido bien, como en casa. Era mi regreso a casa. Pelear es lo que hago desde niño, y es lo que se me da bien. No te acostumbras a sufrir un corte de peso, a pasar hambre, a pasar sed, pero a pelear estamos adaptados. Entonces, estar ahí es como un día más. Lo visualizo cada noche. Lo visualizo cada segundo. Estoy todo el día en el gimnasio entrenando, peleando con mis compañeros. Subirme al octágono es un momento más de mi vida", reconoció. Con apenas 24 años, el peleador español ha demostrado que tiene todo lo necesario para brillar en WOW FC, y después de tomarse casi un año de descanso y regresar por todo lo alto ya tiene un objetivo en mente: volver a principios de 2027 en WOW Bilbao. Aunque tiene claro el lugar y la fecha, lo que le da igual es el rival, ya que su meta no es un nombre en concreto, sino superarse a sí mismo. "De la misma forma que lo enfoco en el combate, no pretendo nada. Yo sé lo que soy. Sé a lo que aspiro y sé dónde voy a llegar. El tiempo y Dios me pondrá a cada paso en el camino, sin pretenderlo. Fluir. Esa es la mentalidad que he adoptado. El agua que fluye nunca se pudre, así que que todo llegue a mí", finalizó.

articles.title: Anthony Yarde still targeting long-awaited showdown with Joshua Buatsi if he beats Willy Hutchinson
articles.summary: Anthony Yarde still wants to make the long-awaited fight with Joshua Buatsi happen; Buatsi takes on Willy Hutchinson for the WBC light heavyweight world title on November 7 in Manchester
articles.body:
Two years on from their first fight back in 2024, Buatsi takes on Hutchinson on November 7 at the AO Arena in Manchester.

Buatsi emerged victorious in their first meeting after dropping Hutchinson twice then winning via decision.

Now, Yarde is backing Buatsi to claim the win because that means they are one step closer to finally meeting in the ring.

Yarde has long been linked with a fight against his fellow light-heavyweight, with the two men seemingly on a collision course ever since Buatsi turned professional after winning bronze at the 2016 Olympics in Rio de Janeiro.

However, the fight, up until this point, has never materialised.

"I have shown time and time again I'm willing to fight anybody and as soon as it got to the point where the public, the pundits and everybody was calling for this fight, I said let's make it happen," said Yarde. "It just makes sense.

"I would have probably rather fought Buatsii in England, a bigger fight for a world title, than go to Saudi Arabia.

"It is a different crowd, different environment and fight [David] Benavidez or even [Artur] Beterbiev, I would have preferred the Buatsi fight over all of them.

"I am not saying because it's an easier fight or anything like that, it is because in my opinion it was a bigger fight."

While Yardley is backing Buatsi in the ring, he thinks his opponent Hutchinson outdoes him in the "entertainment" category by some distance.

"Buatsi is as boring as watching paint dry outside of the ring," he added.

"Because of the public, the Buatsi fight would just make more sense. I would probably want him to win so me and him could fight for a world title.

"But in terms of entertainment outside of the ring, which I think is very important, Hutchinson makes sense as well."

articles.title: Daniel Cormier explains to Sean O'Malley why his name wasn't mentioned at UFC 333
articles.summary: UFC commentator Daniel Cormier explains to Sean O'Malley why he didn't mention him as a potential challenger for Petr Yan at UFC 333.
articles.body:
Sean O'Malley and his head coach, along with many fans, were bothered by Daniel Cormier's handling of the aftermath of UFC 333's co-main event.

Cormier, a retired former UFC champion now a color commentator for the UFC, stepped into the cage to interview Petr Yan , who has defended his UFC bantamweight title in a thrilling trilogy bout against Merab Dvalishvili . Cormier asked Yan (21-5 MMA, 13-4 UFC) if he wanted to face Song Yadong, who was in attendance, but made no mention of O'Malley (20-3 MMA, 12-3 UFC) – who many see as the No. 1 contender in the division.

"The other day, Petr Yan defends his title, and Song Yadong is in the arena, and I said, 'Well, Song Yadong is right there,' because if I'm being completely honest with you, the truck is in my ear saying, 'We're going to show Song,' so then obviously I'm going to say Song Yadong is right there in the arena," Cormier said on his YouTube channel , speaking to O'Malley. "Your coach took a little offense to it, who by the way, I'm going to talk to him tomorrow on his podcast. I messaged you, and you immediately said, 'I don't take it personally; there's no deal. It is what it is.'"

O'Malley and Cormier were very friendly in their conversation and made it clear there was no animosity between the two, several days removed from UFC 333. However, that wasn't O'Malley's initial reaction, and the incident was part of something that O'Malley had been feeling for some time now before clearing things up.

"At the beginning of my career, I felt like, the Terrion Ware fight, I felt, I can't even go back and pinpoint certain moments, but there were times when I was like, 'Man, does DC not really f*ck with me? Does he want to see me lose?'" O'Malley said. "Part of me had that kind of feeling over the course of fights, and it was early on in my career. I was early 20s, young kid, and then you put it in perspective, and you guys are sitting there eight, nine, 10 hours, commentating every single fight, every single card, and you're bound to say something you don't mean or it comes off the wrong way."

O'Malley is currently on a two-fight winning streak since losing his UFC title and failing to recapture it in a pair of championship fights against Dvalishvili. That streak includes a January win over Song (24-9-1 MMA, 13-4-1 UFC), and a June win over Aiemann Zahabi.

Keeping in mind that both O'Malley and Yan have beaten Song, Cormier does see O'Malley as the most deserving challenger for Yan, and regrets not mentioning him at UFC 333.

"Like I said, Song Yadong is in the building. You have beat Song Yadong, and honestly, in that moment, I actually forgot that you beat Song Yadong," Cormier explained to O'Malley. "You got a victory over Song Yadong, and then you got a victory, obviously, at the White House. And after the White House, if you watch the fight, me, Joe (Rogan) Jon (Anik), and I believe we're saying we think Sean should fight for the belt right now, but that didn't happen."

O'Malley feels uber confident his next fight will be for the belt, despite the momentum Yadong has picked up as of late. He feels he doesn't even need to put himself out there to secure a rematch with Yan.

"I don't think it's really a debate or argument, really," O'Malley said. "I mean, you said it. Song was in the building, they were in your ear, it makes sense. I'm not there; Song is there. But I don't think I really have to push for it or argue for it or try to do anything crazy for it. Me vs. Petr is happening next. It just is. I refuse to believe otherwise."

articles.title: Arman Tsarukyan Reveals UFC’s November Deadline for Justin Gaethje, Eyes Alexander Volkanovski Fight
articles.summary: Ahead of UFC 333, Arman Tsarukyan talked about Justin Gaethje's future and welcomed Alexander Volkanovski superfight for 155lbs gold.
articles.body:
Arman Tsarukyan finds himself in a familiar position once again. After spending nearly two years in the UFC's doghouse following his withdrawal from UFC 311 against Islam Makhachev, the Armenian seemed destined to get the next shot at the lightweight title.

Since that infamous pullout, Tsarukyan has done more than enough to make his case. He has scored two finishes, including a win over Dan Hooker at UFC Qatar and a first-round demolition of Mauricio Ruffy at UFC 331 .

However, Alexander Volkanovski's title defense against Movsar Evloev at UFC 333 and his push for a third shot at lightweight gold in a potential retirement fight against Justin Gaethje have complicated things. Amid all this, Tsarukyan has shared a major update on Gaethje's future and revealed that he is open to welcoming the Australian back to lightweight for a fight.

Arman Tsarukyan Explains Why Alexander Volkanovski Would Be the Perfect Matchup for Him

Speaking to Helen Yee ahead of RAF 14, Tsarukyan said, "Someone is trying to duck me; it's Justin Gaethje. Now he's talking about retirement. Either UFC is going to pay him so much money that he's going to fight, or he's just going to retire."

Tsarukyan also revealed that the UFC plans to clarify Gaethje's future by the end of November. Meanwhile, he has no problem taking on Volkanovski if the opportunity arises.

He said, "They told me they're going to let me know at the end of November. I would fight [Volkanovski]. I think it's a good fight for me stylistically. He's old, bad chin. He's a tough opponent, but he's a little bit old now, and with me, it's a perfect fight."

Dana White has admitted that it would be difficult to turn down Volkanovski's request, although the UFC CEO has yet to confirm whether the Australian will get his wish. If Gaethje decides to retire instead, Tsarukyan is ready to step in and face Volkanovski.

The Australian has also recently discussed a potential rematch with Ilia Topuria if Gaethje hangs up his gloves. Tsarukyan, however, has previously expressed his willingness to drop to 145 pounds to fight for featherweight gold, giving the UFC another option to consider.

If Gaethje and Volkanovski end up out of the lightweight title picture, Tsarukyan could find himself in the mix for a vacant title fight. Topuria, Paddy Pimblett, and Charles Oliveira are among the other names who could enter the conversation.

After months of waiting for another opportunity to fight for the 155-pound title, Tsarukyan could finally be approaching a breakthrough. Whether the UFC gives him the long-awaited title shot or another high-profile matchup remains to be seen.

articles.title: Amanda Serrano to face Skye Falzon in final fight with 12 three-minute rounds in Puerto Rico homecoming
articles.summary: Seven-division world champion and Puerto Rico's first and only undisputed boxing champion Amanda Serrano is to defend her unified featherweight world titles against Australia's Skye Falzon in a historic homecoming; fight will be 12 three-minute rounds
articles.body:
Serrano will defend her unified WBO and WBA featherweight world titles at the Coliseo de Puerto Rico in San Juan against Australian contender Falzon, 12-2 (7), over 12 three-minute rounds, under equal championship rules to men.

Not only that, she will be seeking to break the all-time women's knockout record.

Serrano is a Guinness World Record holder for winning world titles across seven weight divisions and the first and only Puerto Rican boxer, male or female, to become undisputed world champion.

Serrano made history alongside Katie Taylor in the first women's boxing match to headline Madison Square Garden in 2022 and then their historic rivalry continued with a rematch in 2024 followed by a trilogy fight that headlined an all-women's card at Madison Square Garden in 2025.

She also made history in 2023 by competing in the first women's unified world championship bout over 12 three-minute rounds, later voluntarily vacating her WBC title rather than abandon her commitment to competing under equal rules to male champions.

Serrano said: "Boxing has been my life and I never could have imagined the journey it would take me and my family on.

"From the early days when women's boxing was fighting for recognition in small theatre shows, to headlining Madison Square Garden in New York, reaching millions of fans around the world on the biggest shows, and helping open doors for the next generation of female fighters, Jordan [Maldonado, Serrano's manager and trainer] and I always believed and I'm proud of everything we've accomplished. But none of it happened alone.

"Nakisa [Bidarian], Jake [Paul] and MVP believed in me and in women's boxing, and together we've helped change what's possible for women in this sport.

"We've fought for respect, equal opportunities, fair pay, and the choice to compete under the same rules as men. There's still more work to do, and I'll continue fighting for the next generation long after I hang up my gloves.

"To close my career at home in Puerto Rico, in front of the people who have supported me from the beginning, means everything."

Nakisa Bidarian and Jake Paul, founders of Most Valuable Promotions, added: "Amanda Serrano is the MOAT. The Most Of All Time. The most accomplished female boxer of all time, the most watched, the most paid, and one of the most influential athletes this sport has ever seen.

"When Amanda became MVP's first signee, we made a commitment to build a platform where the greatest female fighters in the world could receive the recognition, compensation and opportunities they deserve.

"Amanda has been the foundation of that vision, and her success has helped change the entire landscape of women's boxing."
